notes: Chapter 4 drills (D087-D094). Numeric answers are verified by tests/test_drills.py against drill_checks_ch04.py. All scenario facts are hypothetical.

drills.title: Annualizing a quarterly GDP decline
drills.question: Real GDP fell 0.6% quarter on quarter. What annualized rate will the BEA report, and how far is it from the simple 4 x q approximation?
drills.solution: a = (1 + q)^4 - 1 = (0.994)^4 - 1 = -2.3785%. Simple approximation 4 x -0.6% = -2.40%. Compounding makes the decline 0.0215 points smaller in magnitude (the gap is 6q^2 + 4q^3 + q^4 = +0.000215).
common_mistakes: Annualizing a number the BEA has already annualized (reporting -9.1% from a headline of -2.4%)
Treating the compounding gap as material at normal growth rates; it is about 2 bp here
drills.intuition: The headline quarterly GDP number is the quarter's change compounded over four quarters; a 0.6% quarterly fall is reported as roughly -2.4%.
drills.takeaway: Always ask whether a growth figure is q/q, annualized or year over year before comparing it with anything.

drills.title: Contributions: investment versus consumption
drills.question: Shares of GDP: consumption 68%, investment 17%, government 17%, net exports -2%. Consumption grows 0.5%, investment falls 10%, government and net exports are unchanged. Give investment's and consumption's contributions and GDP growth, in percentage points.
common_mistakes: Weighting the components equally
Reading the 10% investment decline as a 10% hit to GDP
drills.intuition: A sixth of GDP that swings 10% outweighs two-thirds of GDP that moves half a percent.
drills.takeaway: Recessions are usually investment events; ask which components moved before translating a GDP print into property demand.

drills.title: Sahm rule from raw unemployment rates
drills.question: Monthly unemployment rates for months 1-15 are 3.7, 3.7, 3.6, 3.6, 3.7, 3.7, 3.8, 3.8, 3.8, 3.9, 4.0, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 (%). Compute the Sahm indicator for month 15 (three-month average minus the minimum three-month average of the previous 12 months). Does it signal? Your fund's policy says to stop signing new hotel acquisitions when the rule signals; what do you do with a hotel bid due next week?

rubric: Computes the month-15 average (4.1 + 4.2 + 4.3)/3 = 4.2000 and the window minimum 3.6333 (months 4 and 5), giving 0.5667
States that the rule has signalled (>= 0.50) and that the policy therefore applies
Recognizes the rule as recognition, not forecast: the recession may already have begun, so hotel NOI risk is near-term

Does not override the policy on the grounds that the level of unemployment is still low; if an exception is argued, it is documented with a specific reason (for example, a labor-supply-driven rise visible in participation and claims data)

drills.solution: Three-month averages: month 3 = 3.6667, months 4 and 5 = 3.6333, month 6 = 3.6667 ... month 15 = 4.2000. Window for month 15 = months 3-14; minimum 3.6333. S = 4.2000 - 3.6333 = 0.5667 >= 0.50: the rule signals. Under the policy the bid is withdrawn or put on hold.
common_mistakes: Using monthly rates rather than three-month averages
Taking the minimum of the raw monthly rates (3.6), which gives 0.60
Treating a low level of unemployment as evidence against the signal
drills.intuition: The rule measures the change in unemployment, which captures the labor-income loop; the level is irrelevant.
drills.takeaway: A pre-committed rule is valuable because it cannot be argued away in the meeting where it matters.

drills.title: Payroll beat, household survey miss
drills.question: Payrolls beat consensus by 60,000, but the prior two months were revised down 90,000, household-survey employment fell 300,000 and the unemployment rate rose 0.2 point. Two-year yields fall 8 bp. Explain the market reaction and what you would check next.

rubric: Computes the effective payroll surprise including revisions: +60,000 - 90,000 = -30,000, so the report is weaker than consensus on the level of employment
Notes that the household survey is noisier month to month but can turn first near cycle peaks; a 0.2-point rise moves the Sahm indicator
Explains the yield fall as the market weighting revisions and the unemployment rate over the headline
Names the next checks: initial jobless claims trend, the Sahm indicator value, wage growth and hours, and whether the household weakness is in participation or in employment

drills.solution: The headline beat is offset by revisions (effective surprise -30,000) and the household survey and unemployment rate point to weakness. Front-end yields fall because the probability of policy easing rose. Check claims, hours, and the Sahm reading before concluding either way.
common_mistakes: Reading the headline beat alone
Dismissing the household survey because it is noisy, without checking whether claims confirm it
drills.intuition: Markets trade the revision to the level of employment, not the headline change.
drills.takeaway: Compute the effective surprise before interpreting any payroll reaction.

drills.title: Inverted curve, base rate, and a floating-rate hotel
drills.question: Your prior that a recession starts within 12-18 months is 20%. The curve has inverted. Assume P(inversion | recession) = 0.90 and P(inversion | no recession) = 0.15. Compute the posterior. A sponsor's hotel acquisition with floating-rate debt works only if the recession probability is below 25%. Decide.

rubric: Notes that the false-positive rate is uncertain (small sample; 1966 and 2022-24 episodes) and shows the posterior remains far above 25% even at a 25-30% false-positive rate
Concludes that the deal as structured should not proceed, or only with lower leverage, a fixed rate or long cap, and a price based on trough NOI
Does not claim certainty of recession; frames the answer as a scenario weight

drills.solution: P(R|Inv) = 0.9 x 0.2 / (0.9 x 0.2 + 0.15 x 0.8) = 0.18/0.30 = 60%. Even with a 30% false-positive rate the posterior is 0.18/(0.18 + 0.24) = 43%. The deal's 25% tolerance is breached; restructure or pass.
common_mistakes: Reading 90% hit rate as 90% recession probability
Ignoring the base rate
drills.intuition: The signal's value depends on how often it appears without a recession, not only on how often it appears before one.
drills.takeaway: Translate every indicator into a likelihood ratio and an explicit posterior before it enters an IC memo.

drills.title: Hotel NOI and DSCR in a recession
drills.question: A hotel has total revenue of $12.0m, fixed costs of $4.2m, and variable costs (including fees and a 4% FF&E reserve) of 35% of revenue. Annual debt service is $2.4m. A recession cuts revenue 12%. Compute recession NOI, the percentage change in NOI, and the DSCR.
common_mistakes: Applying the 12% revenue decline to NOI one-for-one (-12%)
Using GOP or EBITDA instead of NOI after reserve for the DSCR
Forgetting that fees and reserve vary with revenue while labor minimums and taxes do not
drills.intuition: Hotel fixed costs do not shrink with revenue, so NOI falls about twice as fast as revenue.
drills.takeaway: Size hotel debt on trough NOI; a 1.50x DSCR at the peak is about 1.1x in an ordinary recession.

drills.title: SLOOS tightening to a refinancing gap
drills.question: Of 70 SLOOS respondents, 5 tightened CRE standards considerably, 21 somewhat, 40 were unchanged and 4 eased somewhat. Compute the net percentage tightening. Your building has NOI of $1.5m and a $13.5m loan maturing. New terms: value at a 7.5% cap, max LTV 60%, min DSCR 1.35x at 7.0% on 30-year amortization, min debt yield 10%. Compute the maximum loan and the refinancing gap.
common_mistakes: Counting only 'considerably' responses
Excluding 'unchanged' banks from the denominator
Taking the largest rather than the smallest constraint
drills.intuition: Breadth of tightening in the survey shows up at the property level as a lower LTV on a lower value.
drills.takeaway: Run the maturity test early; the gap usually grows as the cycle proceeds.

drills.title: Contradictory data, one-week deadline: the case for abstaining
drills.question: A seller wants a firm, non-contingent bid on a 200-room urban hotel within seven days, at a 7.5% cap on trailing NOI. Advance GDP is +2.5% annualized, but inventories contributed 1.8 points; GDI for the prior quarter was -0.4%; the Sahm indicator is 0.42; the 10y-3m curve has re-steepened 60 bp from deep inversion as markets price cuts; market RevPAR is -4% year over year. The seller provides one year of P&Ls and no property-condition report. What do you do?

rubric: Identifies that underlying demand (GDP ex-inventories about +0.7%), GDI, the Sahm reading and market RevPAR all point toward elevated recession risk, while headline GDP is the only strong datum
Recognizes that the information gap (one year of P&Ls, no PCR, no contingencies) creates adverse selection that cannot be priced in a week
Shows that a 7.5% cap on trailing NOI becomes a much lower yield on recession NOI given hotel operating leverage near 2x
Concludes that the best answer is to abstain from a firm bid, or to offer only a conditional bid (diligence period, three years of P&Ls, price based on trough NOI) that the seller may reject
States what would change the decision: full diligence access, a lower price, or data that lower the recession probability (claims and household employment stabilizing, Sahm reading below 0.30)

drills.solution: This is a deliberately unfavorable combination: high and rising recession probability, the most cyclical property type, a price based on trailing NOI, and no diligence. Abstention, or a conditional bid the seller is free to refuse, dominates. A firm bid at the asking terms earns no credit regardless of the argument offered.
common_mistakes: Anchoring on headline GDP
Treating the curve's re-steepening as an all-clear when it reflects priced rate cuts
Bidding to 'stay in the deal flow' without a price that works on trough NOI
drills.intuition: When the macro evidence and the information asymmetry point the same way, the option to wait is worth more than the deal.
drills.takeaway: Abstention is a position. Write down the conditions under which you would re-engage.
